chapters.relation: Byron and Wood use Marx's claim that the modern state is 'a committee for managing the common affairs of the bourgeoisie' to read House of Cards: Raymond Tusk secretly dictates President Walker's policies, SanCorp buys influence over Frank through Claire's water-filters favor, and Frank's rise to the vice presidency is engineered by capitalists to protect their market interests. Even Frank's seemingly pro-worker America Works plan serves capital, since gutting Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid to subsidize $45,000 hiring costs boosts business profit, and the Dunbar-Walmart dispute shows the state arbitrating between conflicting capitalists rather than aiding workers. The chapter concludes that worker victories like a Dunbar minimum-wage win would only be the bourgeoisie losing a battle while winning the class war, confirming Frank's line that 'democracy is so overrated.'

Sirvent and Diorio apply Foucault's panopticon (built on Bentham's prison design) to the show's web of watching: Frank manipulates Zoe through leaked stories, Doug keeps Rachel permanently locatable by phone, and Claire must demand the bug be removed from Michael Corrigan's Russian cell, showing watched subjects paralyzed by fear. Against Bauman and Lyon's 'liquid surveillance,' the chapter argues democracy is an anti-institutional force requiring free dissent and a press at arm's length from power, and that surveillance collapses the Greek public/private distinction so citizens fear punishment for questioning rulers. Frank's 'Nobody can hear you. Nobody cares about you' to Zoe captures how the surveillance state turns criticism into danger, leaving a society that is no longer a democracy.

chapters.file: ch24 - PART V INTRAPERSONAL RELATIONSHIPS, SEXUALITY, AND RACE IN HOUSE OF CARDS.md

chapters.relation: Southworth and Tallman defend the Underwood marriage by way of Richard Wasserstrom's three grounds for condemning adultery (promise breaking, deception, pain): Frank and Claire's openly negotiated nonmonogamy - Frank disclosing the Zoe affair over breakfast, the Meechum threesome, Claire's nights with Adam Galloway - breaks no promise and involves minimal deception, so it is morally permissible. They reject Vincent Punzo's dualist claim that sex must merge souls, arguing that view rests on unverifiable theology and sets people up for guilt. The marriage's real strength is its egalitarian mutuality - Claire's sabotage of the watershed bill works as tit-for-tat strategy that restores the partnership - and agreed nonmonogamy suits Frank's bisexuality better than monogamy, which would force him to give up part of what it means to be Frank.

Rivera Berruz argues that Freddy Hayes's storyline - the BBQ joint whose franchise design keeps linoleum peeling so 'white folks feel like they slumming,' his son's parole violation destroying the deal, and Frank publicly dropping him when the bad press lands - commodifies black male life as consumable 'spice' for a predominantly white show. Using bell hooks's account of ethnicity as seasoning in commodity culture, Tommy Curry and Michelle Alexander on blackness coded as criminality, and Nancy Leong's racial capitalism, the chapter shows Freddy's value is entirely derivative of his usefulness to Underwood. It closes by adopting Derrick Bell's racial realism ('I live to harass white folks') as the proper stance: the critique cannot dismantle racial capitalism but can harass the representation so viewers stop assuming the stereotype is 'just the way things are.'

Jackson reads the show through Rousseau's contrast between the general will and a pathological 'corporate will': Frank discards Freddy the moment his criminal past goes viral, Tusk and Walker's old friendship curdles into mutual blackmail, and Remy and Jackie trade intimacy for career protection - all reducing Aristotle's true friendship to friendships of utility and pleasure subordinated to institutions that treat persons as means. Rousseau's account of civilization degrading natural self-love (amour de soi) into vanity (amour-propre) explains why Washington's corporate ethos leaves no friends, only 'loose ends' to be eliminated, from Zoe pushed onto the platform to Doug hunting Rachel. The chapter ends with 'Man is born free, but is everywhere in chains' as the verdict on corporate personhood's conquest of human bonds.

chapters.file: ch28 - PART VI EXISTENTIAL REALITIES SELF-LOVE AND FREEDOM.md

chapters.relation: Cooper reads Frank's one prayer - kneeling to pray 'to myself, for myself' - as a self-love he calls autoeroticism, built on metaphysical atheism, ruthless pragmatism, and happiness as power. Like Glaucon's Ring of Gyges, Frank's atheism removes divine punishment from the moral equation, so the murders of Peter Russo and Zoe Barnes incur only human risk, while his feigned piety at the Peachoid girl's vigil, broken promises to Tusk, and 'cruelty well used' toward Russo exemplify Machiavellian virtu taming fortuna. Against this the chapter sets Augustine's critique of the libido dominandi: Frank's remorse after betraying Freddy ('Do you think I'm a hypocrite?') shows the lust for domination enslaves rather than liberates, the way of the City of Man against the Augustinian freedom of self-giving love.

Hackett contrasts Frank's ethical egoism - acting like an invisible Ring of Gyges wearer who pushes Zoe in front of a train and kills Peter once they cannot be controlled - with Beauvoir's existentialist ethics, in which consciousness is a 'nothing' whose freedom is real only when it wills and sustains the freedom of others. Peter's drunken enslavement and Zoe's freely chosen deal with Frank illustrate the ambiguity of a freedom that is still causally situated, and Frank's Season 3 miscalculations with Jackie, Remy, and Claire show egoism's inability to weigh others' self-interest. Claire's sympathy for Michael Corrigan and her final walkout dramatize her learning Beauvoir's lesson that promoting others' freedom is the condition of one's own, the difference between self-interest and existential freedom.

chapters.file: ch31 - PART VII LET ME BE FRANK WITH YOU AGENCY, AESTHETICS, AND INTENTION.md

chapters.relation: Kajtar asks why viewers root for a double-murdering politician, framing the show through Tamar Gendler's puzzle of imaginative resistance: we would refuse to imagine Zoe's murder narrated as 'brave and noble,' yet House of Cards dissolves that resistance. Using Jenefer Robinson's claim that emotional engagement is necessary for understanding, the chapter shows how the Greenville first-pitch embarrassment, the Fort Sumter swim confession, and above all Frank's fourth-wall asides (telling us the real Gaffney eulogy, admitting 'I despise children') grant voyeuristic intimacy that humanizes him bite by bite - 'that's how you devour a whale.' By the time Frank frames Lucas Goodwin and Corrigan dies, we have adopted the morally deviant perspective, and the chapter warns this is exactly how politicians and artists seduce audiences into values we would otherwise reject.

Kaufmann tests Donald Davidson's reductionism (intentions as belief-desire pairs) against Michael Bratman's planning theory through Frank's scheming: Frank can simultaneously desire revenge on Walker and desire to stay near power, but he cannot intend both, so intention's distinctive consistency, partiality, and control explain why he swallows the snub, delivers the education bill, and adjusts when Claire derails Peter's water bill. Tusk's maxim 'Decisions made on emotions aren't decisions at all' and Frank's patience in destroying Tusk across time illustrate Bratman's point that intentions coordinate temporally extended, cross-temporal agency that mere beliefs and desires cannot. The chapter closes on the Iowa victory speech intercut with Claire closing her bedroom door - the first sign her plans have diverged from Frank's.

Dressen and Taliaferro treat Frank's asides as a 'magical mystery tour' of concealment and disclosure, reading truth in Heidegger's fashion as disclosure rather than correspondence: the opening strangling of the dying dog, the Gaffney eulogy where Frank publicly mourns the father he privately calls 'quiet, timid, almost invisible,' and the tombstone urination ('It makes me seem more human') all play presence against absence to alienate Frank from responsibility. A close reading of five maxims - treading water, being a rock, loathing sleep, loving Claire 'more than sharks love blood,' and 'seem more human' - argues Frank consistently styles himself as barely human, the presidency rather than the person. Iris Murdoch's warning that art makes goodness seem dull and relaxes our moral guard explains why viewers find this fascinating rather than condemning.

chapters.file: ch35 - PART VIII VIRTUE AND CHARACTER IN HOUSE OF CARDS.md

chapters.relation: Johnson sorts Frank's six friendships through Aristotle's three kinds: Freddy and Meechum are friendships of pleasure (ribs and candor; loyalty and sex), while Doug, Cathy Durant, Tusk, and Jackie Sharp are friendships of utility that dissolve when usefulness ends - Jackie endorsing Dunbar being the proof. Even Frank's marriage fails the test of true friendship, since Aristotle holds that only good people can mirror each other's character, and badness corrupts the self-knowledge friendship provides. Because Aristotle deems friendship 'most indispensable for life' and eudaimonia requires virtuous activity joined to good fortune, the chapter ends hoping Frank can still choose the good for its own sake - a hope Claire's walkout after Iowa badly dents.

Auxier asks who is morally worse, judging Frank and Claire by past deeds (Frank's murders of Zoe and Peter), future consequences (a president with the nuclear button), and the subjunctive (what each would do), while tracing Claire's lineage from Lady Macbeth and Elizabeth Urquhart, who assassinates Francis in the British series. Plato's and Aristotle's warning that democracy degenerates into tyranny frames the answer: Frank symbolizes the House, Claire the Senate, both coveting executive power, and Meechum - 'utterly loyal, utterly deadly' - is the military they seduce in the menage a trois and will underestimate. Niebuhr's 'moral mediocrity' of nations, from McCarthyism and the Joe Welch moment to mass incarceration, explains the verdict that neither individual is worse alone: 'they are far worse together,' and the union, not the person, has no decency.

chapters.file: ch38 - President Frank Underwood's White House Staff (Contributors).md

holes.name: Racial Capitalism
holes.what: The process (named by Nancy Leong) of deriving social and economic value from racial identity by commodifying it, so that nonwhiteness has value only insofar as it benefits white institutions.
holes.why: Chapter 26's central claim is that Freddy Hayes's BBQ storyline sells blackness as 'authentic' spice for white consumption - an economy the chapter explicitly names racial capitalism.

holes.name: Derrick Bell
holes.what: Critical race theorist whose 'racial realism' holds that racism is a permanent feature of US society, so resistance should aim at defiant harassment of white supremacy rather than at achieving racial equity.
holes.why: Chapter 26 closes by adopting Bell's racial realism and his Biona MacDonald exemplar ('I live to harass white folks') as the stance from which its critique of Freddy's representation is made.

holes.name: Imaginative Resistance
holes.what: The puzzle (associated with Tamar Szabo Gendler) of why we refuse to imagine morally deviant claims as true within fiction - e.g. that a murder was noble - even though we can imagine dragons and unicorns with ease.
holes.why: Chapter 32 argues House of Cards, through Frank's fourth-wall asides and emotional seduction, deliberately dissolves the viewer's imaginative resistance to rooting for a double-murdering politician.

holes.name: Bratman's Planning Theory of Intention
holes.what: Michael Bratman's anti-reductionist view that intentions are distinct plan-states - partial, consistency-demanding, commitment-bearing - that guide and coordinate action over time, against Davidson's reduction of intention to belief and desire.
holes.why: Chapter 33 explains Frank's entire political scheming through the Davidson-Bratman debate over whether intentions are anything more than beliefs and desires.

holes.name: Iris Murdoch
holes.what: Novelist-philosopher who argued that art fascinates by exploring 'the meaner, more peculiar aspects of our being,' leading audiences to relax their moral guard and become lazy sentimental spectators of fictional evil.
holes.why: Chapter 34 uses Murdoch to explain why viewers find Frank's fake eulogy, cruelty, and grave-urination entertaining rather than condemnable.

holes.name: Truth as Disclosure (aletheia)
holes.what: Heidegger's account of truth as unconcealment or disclosure of being, rather than correspondence between statement and fact.
holes.why: Chapter 34 reads Frank's asides, eulogies, and maxims as plays of concealment and disclosure that make truth an event of being, its central Heideggerian move with no matching taxonomy slug.
